Response to Reviewer #1
The manuscript titled "Pinpointing the Thermal History of Lunar Basaltic Meteorites in a Nutshell" by
Pierre Vonlanthen and co-authors presents a comprehensive investigation into the thermal history of
lunar basaltic meteorite NWA 479 using Fe-Ni metal blebs. The authors used the microstructural and
chemical characteristics of these metal blebs to trace the complete thermal evolution of the meteor-
ite, including magmatic crystallization, shock reheating, and post-impact cooling. Their main findings
reveal that the Fe-Ni metal blebs can offer new insights into both igneous and impact-induced thermal
events in planetary bodies, even distinctions between lunar day- and nighttime cooling. Additionally,
the thermal history inferred from the blebs' microstructures and chemical compositions supports a
small impact scenario for the meteorite's ejection from the lunar surface. This study provides novel
insights into the thermal history of lunar basaltic meteorites, particularly through the innovative use
of Fe-Ni metal blebs as geothermometers. While Fe-Ni alloys have been previously studied in mete-
oritic research, this paper advances the field by combining microstructural and chemical analyses to
reconstruct a meteorite's thermal history with remarkable detail. The supplementary materials also
provide extensive additional data. However, several major issues need to be addressed, as outlined
below.
Comment (1a). The study uses plagioclase melting as key evidence to estimate peak shock condi-
tions, which are linked to the formation of certain microstructures in Fe-Ni metal blebs. While plagi-
oclase melting is evident from some figures in the supplementary information, the petrographic evi-
dence for plagioclase melting in Figure 3a may be attributed to silicate liquid immiscibility commonly
observed in the mesostasis of lunar basalts. In this case, the dark vesicles are likely Si-rich liquids,
while the brighter domains at the vesicle peripheries are Fe-rich conjugate liquids. Element mapping
of this area could help confirm this interpretation, and it is unlikely that the observed phenomena
are due to impact-induced plagioclase melting.
We agree and thank Reviewer #1 for this comment. Figs 3 and S6 (and the corresponding cap-
tions/text) have been updated accordingly (lines 145-161, S318-S331). The plagioclase glass in me-
teorite NWA 479 contains both vesicles and immiscible Si-rich liquids, which are pervasive throughout
the rock. We were misled by the observation that these liquids also form embayment fillings or
elongated strips within plagioclase, rather than irregular to mushroom or rounded shapes. Vesicles
can be distinguished from Si-rich liquid blobs based on a number of characteristics, including their
much darker tone in high-contrast BSE images, the occurrence of overpressure cracks in nearby
pyroxene formed during pressure release, and the absence of brighter Fe-rich haloes.
We can confirm that the occurrence of late-stage mesostasis pockets in many lunar basalts has a
purely igneous origin. The whole-rock composition of basalt NWA 479, with Mg# = 39.6 (Fagan et
al., 2002), is also consistent with the “immature” residual pockets described by Pernet-Fisher et al.
(2014). However, the features shown in Figs 3b and S6d stand out for several reasons (see also the
additional images below): (1) the occurrence of Si-rich liquid blobs within (or right next to) molten
vesicular plagioclase, (2) the very irregular shapes and extremely uneven distribution of Si-rich liquid
blobs, (3) the associated melting of Fe-rich pyroxene and ilmenite grains, and (4) the absence of
residual mineral growth, e.g., fayalite with symplectitic “sieve” texture. We therefore argue that the
observed features reflect shock-induced melting rather than liquid immiscibility during igneous cool-
ing. For instance, the Si-rich liquids haloed by more Fe-rich areas are generated at the interface
between plagioclase glass and Fe-rich pyroxene/ilmenite. This observation is more consistent with a
melting process involving the excess heat generated by large differences in shock impedance be-
tween pyroxene/ilmenite and plagioclase, than with a “dissociation” of pyroxene or ilmenite into
differentiated liquids on late-stage igneous cooling. Then, the Si-rich liquids assume the form of
mushroom-shaped blobs reminiscent of “diapiric” intrusions into plagioclase melt. The irregular
shapes and uneven distribution indicate extreme textural immaturity, in good agreement with very
rapid quenching immediately after shock. In the event of comparatively slow igneous cooling, we
would have anticipated more “stable” blob shapes and textures. In addition, the conjugate melting
of Fe-rich phases (pyroxene rims, ilmenite) and plagioclase results in the formation of immiscible
liquids, as experimentally shown by Rutherford et al. (1974) for other purposes. Finally, the associ-
ation of Si-rich blobs with plagioclase glass observed here is not comparable to the “sieve” texture
resulting from the entrapment of Si-rich melt droplets during late-stage crystal (e.g., fayalite) growth
in mesostasis pockets (Pernet-Fisher et al., 2014).
Additional BSE images from our subsample of meteorite NWA 479. a Field of view containing vesicles (associated with overpres-
sure cracks, as in Figs 3a and S6a,b) and Si-rich liquid blobs (in medium gray within light-gray plagioclase glass, as in Figs 3b
and S6d). b Partial melting of (idiomorphic) pyroxene grains in contact with plagioclase glass. The Si-rich liquid blobs are sur-
rounded by slightly brighter Fe-rich haloes. c Close-up view of b displaying the extremely irregular shapes and uneven distribution
of the Si-rich liquid blobs generated at the interface with the Fe-rich pyroxene rims. d Replica of Figs 3b and S6d summarizing
most of the features shown from a to c. Note that the black spot labeled “vesicle” crosscuts the Si-rich liquid blob to the right, in
good agreement with the idea of shock-induced melting of plagioclase (and nearby pyroxene) associated with vesiculation upon
pressure release. Unfortunately, it is no longer possible to obtain a close-up image of this specific location due to the additional
polishing step (involving the removal of a layer of material) required for EBSD analyses (see lines S738-S739). Accordingly, the
“vesicle” was not labeled in Figs 3b and S6d.
In conclusion, we do not contest the characteristics of the late-stage mesostasis pockets as re-
ported in the literature, but we believe that the features shown in Figs 3b, S6d (and above) are of a
different nature. Our analysis indicates that these features reflect shock-induced melting of Fe-rich
minerals (pyroxene, ilmenite) in contact with hot vesiculated plagioclase glass in a process facilitated
by large differences in shock impedance. In this respect, the presence of the Si-rich liquid blobs
serves to reinforce our interpretation and the scenario of a high (near-)equilibrium peak-shock tem-
perature.
Comment (1b). The authors estimate a peak-shock temperature of 660-690 °C and suggest that this
estimate is consistent with the observed microstructures, such as “occasional recrystallization of the
rim into deformation-free fcc twin lamellae, annealing of bcc grains within the cores” (Line 568-570).
However, the presence of high-pressure minerals like ringwoodite and wadsleyite in the same mete-
orite (Barrat et al., 2005) complicates this estimation. While using these high-pressure minerals to
estimate peak shock conditions may be questionable, they can set an upper limit on the post-shock
temperature, as they would retrograde to low-pressure polymorphs if temperatures were sufficiently
high after pressure release (Hu and Sharp, 2022). It would be beneficial to assess whether the
estimated peak-shock temperature aligns with the preservation of high-pressure minerals in the me-
teorite.
This is a highly pertinent and timely issue. Two additional paragraphs have been included in the
supplementary materials (lines S345-S362).
It is true that Barrat et al. (2005, p. 5600) identified ringwoodite and wadsleyite in some olivine rock
fragments entrained in the shock melt veins of meteorite NWA 479. However, “despite [the] acquisi-
tion of >40 [Raman] spectra within [the] shock melted regions”, Mijajlovic et al. (2020, p. 2278) did
not document any such high-pressure minerals in paired meteorite NWA 032, while Miyahara et al.
(2019, p. 6014) reported the occurrence of ringwoodite in close proximity to shock-melt veins in the
very same rock. While the results differ, we believe that none of these authors are incorrect or have
overlooked the petrological aspects of their work. In our opinion, this is an excellent illustration of
the importance of the P-T-t path is, and how it can vary on a very local scale within the same (or
paired) sample(s). This is particularly relevant for high-pressure minerals, as their formation and
preservation are closely tied to shock melt veins and pockets, in which the P-T-t path can vary dras-
tically and over very short distances. Thus, we fully agree with Hu and Sharp (2022) and with the
growing consensus that the local P-T-t path is a crucial consideration when studying the shock history
of meteorites. Actually, the potential shortcomings of high-pressure minerals and the necessity for
more reliable indicators were key factors that prompted the present study.
In meteorite NWA 479, the time of “~1 s or more” (now “at least 1 s”, lines 497 and S678) to
reach the equilibrium (or near-equilibrium, see below) peak-shock temperature of 660-690°C
throughout the rock (including the thickest shock melt veins, the plagioclase glass, the rock-forming
silicates, and the Fe-Ni metal blebs), was calculated by solving the Stefan problem (lines S658-
S679). Given that the entire shock pulse only lasted between 10-4 to 10-2 s (lines 408-439), the
equilibrium peak-shock temperature (660-690°C) was reached after pressure release (lines 458-
468). Our calculations also indicate that post-shock cooling from the equilibrium peak-shock temper-
ature (660-690°C) to the residence temperature in space (0-50°C) lasted between seconds and
minutes depending on the initial ejection size of the meteorite (lines 504-514, S711-S722). Further
refinement of this range to tens of seconds is possible when considering the most probable scenario,
in which the percentage of mass loss on atmospheric entry was closer to the average value (70%)
than the end-members (50% and 90%). As stated by Hu and Sharp (2017, p. 277), “experimental
studies of transformation kinetics show that wadsleyite transforms to olivine in seconds at tempera-
tures above 1200 K (~927°C) and in hours at temperatures between 900 K (~627°C) and 1200 K
(~927°C)” at ambient pressure. Similar results for ringwoodite are presented in Table 3 (p. 287). We
therefore argue that our scenario is very well in line with the data presented by Hu and Sharp (2017,
2022) and the preservation of ringwoodite and wadsleyite reported by Barrat et al. (2005). Given
that the equilibrium peak-shock temperature (660-690°C) was reached after “at least 1 s”, and that
the post-shock cooling residence temperature in space (0-50°C) was reached after tens of seconds
(following a logarithmic path), it can be concluded that the critical temperature of ~627°C (900 K)
was crossed very early, after a few seconds at most. This time lapse is two to three orders of mag-
nitude shorter than the necessary duration reported by Hu and Sharp (2017) to retrograde ring-
woodite and wadsleyite into olivine at ambient pressure. Therefore, the local preservation of ring-
woodite and wadsleyite is consistent with our interpretation and scenario.
Conversely, providing a definitive explanation for the crystallization of high-pressure minerals
during such a brief shock pulse may be more challenging. Our interpretation is that the exceptionally
rapid crystallization of these high-pressure polymorphs required very strong kinetics. The tempera-
ture of the shock melt veins was likely very high, providing sufficient thermal energy to initiate such
rapid phase transformations. Unfortunately, there is no indication regarding the size or preservation
state of ringwoodite and wadsleyite in Barrat et al. (2005). This is because the high-pressure mineral
assemblage was apparently identified through Raman spectra only. This significantly restricts the
ability to ascertain the local prograde and retrograde P-T-t paths from these data. Nevertheless, we
suggest that the high energy required to form high-pressure minerals in such a short time frame
provides further evidence that a globally high-temperature scenario occurred during shock.
Comment (1c). The authors refer to “thermal equilibrium” or “equilibrium peak-shock temperature”
to describe the thermal state of the meteorite. It is important to note that temperature equilibration
occurs on a timescale much longer than pressure equilibration, with millimeter-scale temperature
heterogeneities equilibrating on a timescale of seconds (Sharp and DeCarli, 2006). Although the
authors acknowledge the substantial time required to reach peak-shock thermal equilibrium, their
model oversimplifies the situation by estimating an unrealistic equilibration time of “~1 s or more”.
Given the proposed scenario of “shock reheating followed by rapid post-shock cooling,” it is ques-
tionable whether true thermal equilibrium was ever achieved throughout the rock. Therefore, the
term “equilibrium” should be used with caution in this context.
We agree. The issue of “thermal equilibrium” or “equilibrium peak-shock temperature” was addressed
in four paragraphs (lines 515-579) in the original manuscript. We stated that even if “unequivocal
evidence for which the shock reheating curve would have been superseded by post-shock cooling
has not been found” (lines 515-516), “it cannot be definitively asserted that the blebs located at the
periphery of the meteorite or trapped within large insulating phenocrysts have even reached com-
plete peak-shock thermal equilibrium” (lines 512-514). Accordingly, we acknowledge that the term
"equilibrium" may be interpreted as "near-equilibrium". This has now been clarified in a dedicated
section of the text (lines 531-536).
That said, the equilibration time of “at least 1 s” (following a logarithmic cooling path) calculated
by solving the Stefan problem (lines S658-S679) is in line with the estimate of Sharp and deCarli
(2006, p. 653) that “temperature heterogeneities equilibrate on a timescale of seconds”. Then, from
a terminological standpoint, the term “equilibrium peak-shock temperature” is commonly (and per-
haps abusively) used in the planetary science literature to describe the temperature reached after
thermal equilibration of the rock. This is a generic term that is widely recognized and used by most
planetary scientists, regardless of whether full thermal equilibrium has been reached or verified. In
particular, it allows for the differentiation between the various thermal states (or stages) of the shock
history. These include the pre-shock residence temperature on the planetary body, the instantaneous
and transient temperature anomalies on impact (resulting from pore collapse, friction heating, dif-
ference in shock impedance, planar defects, etc.), and the post-shock thermal equilibrium reached
after cooling in the outer space. Incidentally, it should be noted that thermal equilibrium is reached
asymptotically and theoretically after an infinite period of time, which makes the term somewhat
misleading anyway. In the updated version of the manuscript, we propose to retain the well-known
and widely used expression “equilibrium peak-shock temperature” (together with the explanation in
lines 531-536), even if we acknowledge that full thermal equilibrium might not have been reached.
By doing so, we avoid the risk of confusing the readers even more with a new term of our own, or
with a shortened wording (such as “peak-shock temperature”) that might be misinterpreted with
transient thermal peaks.
Comment (2). I strongly recommend adding explanations for key terminology (e.g., bcc, fcc, hcp)
and phase transformations (e.g., bcc to fcc, bcc to hcp, and martensitic transformation) in the sup-
plementary information. Many planetary scientists may not be familiar with these terms. For instance,
martensitic transformation is uncommon in silicate minerals, making it challenging for readers to
understand how this transformation could kinetically occur under extremely low temperatures (i.e.,
< -100 °C, Line 279-285, Figure 5a). Providing these explanations will enhance the accessibility of
the manuscript.
We agree. The acronyms bcc, fcc, and hcp have been spelled out in full for the first time they are
mentioned in the manuscript (lines 66-67, 352-353). A widely accessible piece of text on martensitic
transformations in the broad sense has been added to the supplementary materials (lines S408-
S418).
Comment (3). The authors derive several critical temperatures based on the phase diagram, such as
90-160 °C during rapid daytime cooling and -160 °C during rapid nighttime cooling. However, uncer-
tainties in these temperature estimates could arise from modifications and shifts in the MF and AF
curves, conversions from ternary to binary concentrations, and the use of averaging rather than
interface compositions. While it is challenging to determine the exact uncertainties, an approximate
estimation of these uncertainties would be valuable.
The extent of the shift applied to MS, MF, AS, and AF was addressed and calculated with regards to
alloying elements (lines S461-S495), particle size (lines S497-S526), grain size (lines S528-S562),
and compression (lines S564-S589). A new paragraph was added to address the influence of Co,
which has the most significant impact on MF and AF. During shock heating for example, a 1.0 wt%
change in Co results in a shift of ~30°C of the transformation curves (lines S479-S488).
Please note that the Fe and Ni concentrations at the interfaces (Fig. 5) are not average values.
Instead, they have been retrieved from the TEM-EDS profiles shown in Fig. 4 (lines 164-165, 446-
447). Only trace elements were averaged (from WDS analyses), first because the TEM-EDS detection
limit in profile mode insufficient for quantifying the trace elements with enough counting statistics,
and then because long analyses in spot mode (or on tiny areas) were found to damage the TEM foil.
For further information on statistical significance and representativeness, please refer to the new
section in the supplementary materials (lines S591-S653).
In our opinion, the primary (but moderate) source of uncertainty is the limited data available for
MF and AF in Fe-Ni alloys, while MS and AS are much better documented. This issue is thoroughly
discussed from a qualitative standpoint (lines S439-S457), but there is not much more we can do to
quantify uncertainties resulting from a lack of data. We believe that the exceptional fit between the
temperatures obtained for igneous cooling and the day- and nighttime temperatures expected for
the early Eratosthenian period (lines 287-294) and that the validation of the high equilibrium peak-
shock temperature scenario by other means (lines S622-S645) are good indicators of reliability.
However, we agree that the precision of our model could be enhanced through further research, such
as the analysis of Fe-Ni metal blebs trapped in returned lunar samples. Given the well-established
location and depth of these samples, they would be ideal for fine-tuning the igneous cooling temper-
atures. Nevertheless, in light of the aforementioned discussion and the new sections added to the
supplementary materials, we think that the issue of uncertainties has been addressed as thoroughly
as possible.
Comment (4). The manuscript describes various stages of deformation of the Fe-Ni blebs. However,
it is not clear how the authors differentiate between deformation features related to igneous cooling
(Line 305-321) and those resulting from subsequent shock imprints. Providing an explanation of how
these features are distinguished would be beneficial for understanding the deformation processes.
The differentiation between igneous and shock deformation features was primarily based on the
magnitude and nature (e.g., concentric fracturing) of deformation (see also the sketches and related
texts in Fig. 5). We acknowledge that unequivocal distinction at the local scale is difficult because
the slip systems that were activated during igneous cooling were probably reactivated during shock.
Nevertheless, even if some overlap probably exists, the notable differential volumetric changes of
the Fe-Ni metal blebs on igneous cooling cannot be inconsequential on the crystal lattice (see below
and lines 313-330). However, they were much too weak to explain cumulative misorientations of up
to 50° degrees observed in the rims (Figs S3 to S5).
It is important to note that the crystal lattices of silicates and metals do not respond to cooling in
the same way, in accordance with the amount of internal strain underwent by either type of materials.
In the former, igneous processes rarely result in significant lattice deformation because the strain
induced by magmatic cooling is low. As an example, basalt exhibits a volumetric change between
1000°C and 0°C of ~1-2% (Hartlieb et al., 2016), which means that the minimal differential stress
between minerals can be accommodated by other means, such as grain boundary sliding and/or
fracturing. With metals, however, the situation is different. First, the volumetric change within the
same temperature range of 1000°C to 0°C is much larger, ~10% in pure iron for example (Basinski
et al., 1955). Then, the expansion coefficients at a given temperature can vary significantly for the
same type of alloys. For instance, Fe-Ni metals with an Invar composition (~64 wt% Fe, ~36 wt%
Ni) demonstrate minimal volumetric change when exposed to temperature variations below 100°C.
In contrast, Fe-Ni alloys with compositions other than Invar demonstrate significant expansion and
contraction. Finally, the martensitic transformations commonly observed in metals are also accom-
panied by sudden volumetric changes, in the order of ~4 % in Fe-Ni alloys. Therefore, metals are
subject to stronger internal strain on cooling than silicates, resulting in deformation of a few degrees
of the crystal lattice. Deformation can be accommodated plastically at high temperatures and in a
more and more fragile way upon cooling. In the present case, the contraction gaps provided some
additional flexibility to accommodate volumetric changes, but not enough to fully compensate for the
internal deformation of the Fe-Ni metal blebs.
In contrast, cumulative misorientations up to several tens of degrees, such as those observed in
the Fe-Ni metal rims, require strong perturbations of the stress field. In the absence of regional
tectonics and metamorphism, these conditions can only result from the shock waves generated on
impact. The resulting features are large cumulative misorientations within grains, which are still
visible today in the rims (Figs S3 to S5).
Comment (5). The manuscript includes a depiction of the fcc-to-bcc transformation of Fe-Ni blebs
upon cooling in space (Figure 5). This transformation is relevant to the section on “Shock Reheating
Followed by Rapid Post-Shock Cooling.” However, the text does not address this transformation pro-
cess. Including a discussion on this transformation in the relevant section would provide a more
comprehensive understanding of the observed phenomena.
We agree (lines 570-579).
Line 23: A space is needed before “°C” here and also at other places.
According to the “Chicago Manual of Style – The Essential Guide for Writers, Editors and Publishers”,
comprehensive 1200-page reference on English writing: “a space is normally used between the nu-
meral and the unit of measure, except in a few cases, for example degree, percent and prime sym-
bols: 50 km, 21 ha, 4.5 l, but 10.5°C”. I am afraid that there is no need for a space here, even
though the SI system allows for one. Of course, a space is needed when written in full: “10.5 degrees
Celsius”.
Line 26-27: “peak temperature was reached…mainly by thermal conduction from hot vesicular pla-
gioclase”. See the major comment 1
See reply to Comment 1
Line 28-29: The phrase "We propose… for lunar meteorites" could be rephrased to clarify the con-
nection between the findings and previous models, as it feels slightly abrupt.
We agree. The abstract has been fully rephrased to comply with the 150-word policy (lines 13-23).
Line 196 thick enough?
We agree. The sentence has been rephrased (line 193-194).
Line 205-207: references are needed here. The graphite oxidation process is also suggested to be

Line 240-242 The early crystallized olivine and pyroxene would preferentially incorporate Mg over
Fe. This selective incorporation of Mg actually leads to a relative enrichment of Fe in the remaining

Line 246-249 As early crystallization phases, the current relative positions of Fe-Ni blebs and chro-

Line 283-285 This sentence is a little difficult to read, I would suggest changing it to “Hence, our

Response to Reviewer #2
The paper Pinpointing the thermal history of lunar basaltic meteorites in a nutshell by Vonlanthen et
al. presents microscopic metallurgical characterization of the iron-nickel alloy blebs in lunar mare
basalt NWA 479. They observed nanoscale fcc-to-bcc transition in the alloy and proposed a marten-
sitic transformation model to constrain the thermal history of lava on lunar surface. The authors
further described the bcc-to-fcc inversion (as austenitic) and used that to constrain the potential
shock heating of the sample. While the data are detailed and figures / cartoons are very well made,
there are a few uncertainties that could jeopardize the development of Fe-Ni phases into a robust
geothermometer. The findings, although quite interesting and worth publication, has yet to demon-
strate universal usefulness for geological samples as high-impact results. My questions about the
results and interpretations are listed below:
Comment (1) One key conclusion of the work is the confirmation of a small-impact launch of the
sample, suggested by the shallow depth of its pre-impact setting, which in turn is interpreted from
the assumption that the sample experienced lunar day-dusk temperature difference that results in
the fcc-to-bcc transition at blow 0 °C on 29.7 wt% Ni. If the model is correct, thus observation should
be consistent through the whole sample and backed by more than one singular FIB section of alloy.
(It looks like bleb 3 was FIB cut, but no profile data.)
To address this important issue, a new section has been added to the supplementary materials (lines
S591-S653). While we agree in principle with the above comment that the more analyses done, the
more robust the interpretation, we demonstrate that additional high-end analyses (FIB thinning, TEM
BF/DF/HAADF imaging, quantitative TEM-EDS, and ultra-high resolution ACOM/ ASTAR mapping) are
not scientifically justified. Our results and interpretation can be successfully validated (and even
reinforced) using the data (EBSD mapping, WDS analyses, etc.) collected in other eligible blebs, in
addition to being supported by typical microstructural features of the rock. We also show that attain-
ing statistical significance using high-end analytical tools is technically unrealistic (statistics and com-
plexity are inversely correlated), but that this inherent limitation is largely offset by the unprece-
dented results they provide (see also the comments of Reviewer #1). This is particularly the case
when the interpretation and scenario can be validated by other means. The key points are as follows:
a) Our subsample of meteorite NWA 479 contains a total of only seven Fe-Ni metal blebs (Figs S1 to
S5). Four of them were deemed ineligible for use as geothermometers (and therefore excluded
from the high-end analyses), either because they were hollow (i.e., subjected to disproportionate,
shock impedance-related, thermal reaction upon impact; blebs 4, 5, and 6; lines 119-130, 337-
344, S226-S300, Fig. 2), or completely non-representative because of an exceptional size, unu-
sual chemical composition and texture (bleb 7; lines 537-566). Of the three remaining blebs, two
were fibbed, with a successful outcome for bleb 1 (Figs 1, 4, and S3) and a fatal ending for bleb
3 (see point c below and footnote in Table 1). Therefore, of the seven initial blebs, only one, bleb
2, remains as a potential geothermometer.
b) Table 1 shows that bleb 2 is chemically zoned (as are all the Fe-Ni metal blebs in meteorite NWA
049), with a core center and a rim containing 12.30 wt% and 33.18 wt% Ni, respectively (see
Fig. S3 for the locations of WDS analyses). Upon conversion to binary compositions, the Ni con-
centration of the rim is equivalent to ~34 wt%. Then, Fig. S3 illustrates that bleb 2 has a compa-
rable nutshell-like microstructure to that observed in other blebs, comprising a core surrounded
by an intermediate band and a rim. Based on these observations, we can state with a high degree
of confidence that the Ni content at the intermediate band-rim interface is notably smaller than
~34 wt%, and even more so at the core-intermediate band interface. It is therefore very reason-
able (and probably conservative) to assume that the Ni content at the core-intermediate band
interface is ~30 wt% (or less). When plotted in Fig. 5a (the 6th T-XFe-Ni diagram), and after fine-
tuning AF following the method described in Supplementary Section 4, the composition of 30 wt%
Ni indicates an equilibrium peak-shock temperature of ~600°C. Being a bit less conservative with
regard to the Ni content, the value moves towards (or falls within) the range of 660-690°C derived
from the high-resolution TEM-EDS profiles of bleb 1. Even in the unlikely (actually very improba-
ble) event that the Ni content at the core-intermediate band interface would be identical to that
measured in the middle of the rim (~34 wt%), the temperature would still be ~540°C. In conclu-
sion, the temperature estimates retrieved from the data already available from bleb 2 are in very
good agreement with the results obtained from the high-end analyses of bleb 1. Both support the
high equilibrium peak-shock temperature and the scenario proposed in our study. Furthermore,
this convergence of results demonstrates that our interpretation is independent of the location of
the blebs within the meteorite. This provides further evidence that validates the use of Fe-Ni metal
blebs as whole rock geothermometers, and to the interval of 660-690°C as equilibrium (or near-
equilibrium; lines 531-536) peak-shock temperature for meteorite NWA 479.
c) It is also worth noting that the high-temperature scenario upon shock is also supported by other
factors, namely, the pervasive distribution of vesicular plagioclase glass (lines 145-157, lines
S306-S317, Figs 3a and S6a,b,c), the occurrence of irregular, mushroom-shaped, Si-rich liquid
blobs (lines 147-148, S318-S323, Figs 3b and S6d), the local but frequent melting of ilmenite and
pyroxene (Fig. S6e,f), well-developed planar deformation and mosaicism in olivine (lines S379-
S386), unequivocal evidence for massive crystal-plastic deformation in all the types of pheno-
crysts (see below), and large shock melt veins.
d) Please also consider the non-standard character of the sophisticated analytical techniques used
here. We invested a (really) huge amount of time and resources to ensure the successful collection
of the results presented in the manuscript. As an example, the successful clearance of a homo-
geneously thin TEM-transparent FIB foil from a small Fe-Ni metal bleb embedded in silicates with
a contraction gap in between is a tremendously difficult task (note that the foil trace shown in Fig.
1a represents the portion of the foil shown in Fig. 1c, and not the much larger entire foil, as
indicated in lines S786-S787 and specified in the new version of the figure). Silicates and metals
exhibit markedly different abrasion resistance to ions (while the contraction gap has none), which
means that the settings appropriate for one material almost invariably lead to the amorphization
of the other. This is what happened to bleb 3, that was also fibbed and observed by TEM… just to
realize that it had been completely amorphized by the thinning process (footnote in Table 1). It is
only after many trial-and-error sessions on blank samples that we finally succeeded in preparing
one foil ready for TEM imaging/-EDS and ACOM/ASTAR mapping (bleb 1). Then, the lift-out of the
TEM foil from a bleb, which was essentially “suspended in a vacuum” (the contraction gap between
metal and silicates was only disrupted by rare contact points), presented a challenge too. In
summary, the foil of bleb 1 was on a knife edge throughout the entire FIB session. The complexity
of the sample preparation process is likely a contributing factor to the fact that this approach has
not been attempted previously. A similar observation can be made with regard to ACOM/ASTAR.
While this technique is extremely powerful and crucial for obtaining nm-scale crystallographic
orientation mapping, the access to it is limited by its complexity. As a reminder, the objective of
this paper is to pave the way for new solutions to long-standing and contentious issues. We rec-
ognize that these high-end analyses cannot be performed on a routine basis.
e) The use of sophisticated analytical techniques is inherent to lower statistical significance, given
the inverse correlation between the two. Nevertheless, we believe that this drawback is largely
offset by the unparalleled results they provide. This is particularly the case when the interpretation
can be validated by other means, showing that low- and high-end techniques are perfectly com-
plementary. We also We also emphasize that to achieve true statistical significance, the entire set
of analyses conducted in bleb 1 would need to be repeated in tens of Fe-Ni metal blebs eligible as
full geothermometers, collected from as many different subsamples as possible. Such an approach
is clearly unrealistic in terms of the requisite machine time, laboratory access, costs, and so forth.
f) Finally, it should be kept in mind that FIB is destructive: once it is done, the sample has gone
forever. With only one eligible bleb left (bleb 2), and given the high risk of amorphization, we
strongly recommend that it be archived and preserved.
Comment (2) And I am not sure about the meaningfulness of averaging 25 data points in a profile
of continuously changing compositions…
There seems to be a misunderstanding here. The values in Table S1 were averaged over 25 points
separately for each of the six selected portions of the profiles, i.e., the internal part of the core (Ibcc
core), the very external part of the core (Ebcc core), the internal part of the intermediate band (Ibcc
IB), the external part of the intermediate band (Ebcc IB), the very internal part of the rim (Ifcc rim),
and the external part of the rim (Efcc rim) (see the locations of * and † signs in Table S1). Therefore,
the compositions are not “continuously changing”, but constant over the selected portions. As an
example, the composition of the 25 points averaged from the internal part of the core (Ibcc core) is
found to be within the range of 85.0 and 86.5 wt%, with the exception of two “outliers” at ~84 and
~87 wt% (average: 85.8 wt%).
Comment (3) Also, if a few wt% of Fe/Ni would be important for the conclusion, the 4 wt% cobalt
need to be treated more carefully, instead of projecting the Fe/Ni ratio directly on the binary phase
diagram.
That is precisely what we have done! The effect of Co and the other alloying elements Cr, Ca, and Ti
on MS MF, AS, and AF was detailed in the supplementary materials (lines S461-S488, Table S2). Of
course, the results were used to refine the positioning of the transformation curves in Fig. 5. In
regard to the potential errors associated with the Co content, we have included additional information
in the supplementary file (lines S479-S488). Finally, minor (and even moderate) changes in Fe and
Ni concentrations does not at all invalidate the scenario of a high equilibrium peak-shock temperature
(as outlined in point b of the response to comment 1 and lines S622-S645).
Comment (4) In Fig. 5, the reference phase boundaries are clearly shown in at% space while the
axes and chemical data are reported in wt%. The martensitic phase boundary, e.g. in Kaufman and
Cohen 1956, was also reported in at% space originally. Please double check the translation to wt%
is correct.
The caption of Fig. 5 has been updated to clarify (lines 447-448) that all the data presented in tables
or figures (including MS, MF, AS, and AF) were systematically converted into wt% in the original man-
uscript. This also applies to the background boundary lines shown as references in light gray in Fig.
5, which were sourced from Swartzendruber et al. (1991) and Yang et al. (1996) precisely because
they were displayed in wt% (see the figure below). Both papers were referenced in the caption of
Fig. 5. We agree that the field boundary lines displayed in Fig. 5 bear a striking resemblance to those
reported in at% in the literature (including in the paper by Kaufman and Cohen, 1956). However,
this is simply a consequence of the very close atomic weight of Fe and Ni. As an example, a compo-
sition of 60.0/40.0 wt% Fe/Ni is equivalent to 61.1/38.9 at% Fe/Ni.
Fe-Ni phase diagram showing the boundary lines refer-
enced in light gray in Fig. 5 (from Yang et al., 1996). Note
that the compositions are in wt% (as everywhere in our
paper).
Comment (5) In my understanding, EBSD orientation processing requires the user to manually input
whether a high misorientation angle indicates local deformation of one crystal grain or separate
grains. It looks like e.g. bleb 5 rim could represent a bunch of non-twinned grains. And I cannot quite
understand the map of bleb 4, in which there are areas of no-solution in the alloy and with bcc
identification in the silicate glass.
An explanation has been added to the supplementary materials (lines S753-S754) to clarify the
misorientation angle defining boundary lines in EBSD maps.
The issue regarding bleb 5 is explained in the introduction (lines 67-70): “The cores are typically
encased in a single-crystal fcc rim that exhibits smooth and gradual misorientations of up to ~50°,
which suggests deformation under a plastic regime. The sporadic occurrence of sharper misorienta-
tions across (sometimes concentric) fractures indicates that the rim was also subject to moderate
semi-brittle deformation”. The “bunch of non-twinned grains” reported in the above comment actu-
ally represents the subgrains created by semi-brittle deformation. Upon examination of the EBSD
misorientation map - fcc (Fig. S4), it is evident that the deformation of the rim of bleb 5 is of a dual
nature. The smooth change in crystallographic orientations on the left hand side of the bleb is indic-
ative of a plastic regime. In contrast, the more acute changes between subgrains on the top and
right sides indicate a more brittle regime (even though the subgrains themselves are plastically de-
formed, hence the use of the term “semi-brittle”). In addition, the overwhelming majority of these
subgrains display respective misorientations smaller than 15° (as indicated by colors ranging be-
tween greenish and yellowish). This indicates that they were generated from the single-crystal rim
(see also the ARPGE results) when the conditions for purely plastic deformation were no longer met.
Similarly, blebs 4 and 6 exhibit comparable characteristics (Fig. S4). The more chaotic microstructure
of the hollow blebs was presented as one of the arguments explaining their collapse upon shock and
their ineligibility as full geothermometers (lines 123-130, S226-S300).
The misunderstanding regarding bleb 4 can be easily resolved by referring to the caption of Fig.
S3 (lines S152-S156), which states, “The minor inconsistencies in bleb morphology observed in the
BSE images and the EBSD maps are due to the additional polishing step required for EBSD analyses”.
This was repeated in the captions of Figs S4 and S5 (lines S204, S220) as follows: “Layout as in Fig.
S3”. The same statement is applicable to all the Fe-Ni metal blebs. As detailed in the supplementary
materials (lines S738-S729), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) requires a surface of analysis
that is free of mechanical damage. This involves an additional chemomechanical polishing using al-
kaline (pH=9.8) aqueous suspension of colloidal silica. It is inevitable that the removal of material
(likely in the range of 100s of nanometers in this case) will become visible when comparing the BSE
images and the EBSD maps acquired before and after the additional polishing step, respectively. It
is important to note that the distinction is readily apparent, given the small scale of the features in
question. If the blebs had been larger (in the range of 100s of micrometers) and imaged at a lower
magnification, the material removed by EBSD polishing would have likely gone unnoticed.
Comment (6) It would also be clearer to include more experimental details such as mapping step,
noise reduction in processing, whether modeled contour is used in the final map and showing a few
representative diffraction patterns.
Step sizes for EBSD (25-50 nm), TEM (1-2 nm), and ACOM/ASTAR (2 nm) maps were already spec-
ified in the supplementary materials (line S747, S796, S808). The noise reduction methods used for
EBSD (lines S748-S752) have been standard since the 1990s. Those used for ACOM/ASTAR are out-
lined in the text (lines S818-S824) and described in greater detail in two dedicated papers (supple-
mentary references 81 and 82).
Regarding the addition of diffraction patterns, please consider the following. Since the early de-
velopments of EBSD in the 1970s and 1980s, the technique has primarily been applied to (bcc and
fcc) metals. The main reason is that metals have historically been and continue to be crucial industrial
materials. Other reasons include the fact that metals are conductive (no charging issue, except when
trapped in non-conductive materials such as silicates) and have a high backscatter coefficient (an
asset when the detectors, or films, had very low sensitivity). During the 1980s and 1990s, tons of
EBSD patterns of fcc and bcc metals were published. We therefore believe that doing so in a Nature
Communications paper to be published in the years 2024-2025 would be inappropriate, outdated,
and unnecessary for the comprehension of the paper.
Comment (7) The abrupt step in composition at intermediate band-rim is interpreted as an igneous
feature that stops the shock-induced inversion. Does that mean the Fe-Ni segregation/diffusion is
also expected spontaneously with martensitic transition? Does the transition create an interface-
controlled diffusion that leads to the abrupt step? Again, more profile data would be helpful.
Sorry, but there is no abrupt step in composition at the intermediate band-rim interface (Fig. 4, Table
S2). We guess that this comment is related to the compositional step at the core-intermediate band
interface. That said, it is right that the martensitic transformations in Fe-Ni metal are accompanied
by a process of “rejection” (or “discharge”) followed by diffusion of Ni towards interstitial fcc grains
of the core and beyond the core outer border. Further clarification has been provided in the revised
manuscript (lines 264-268). This process is also well documented in the steels, where carbon is
expelled during martensitic transformations regardless of the direction of the compositional gradient.
It is also interesting to note that Ni did not effectively “segregate” at grain boundaries (at least
not for an extended period) and was rapidly removed from there (profile BB’ in Fig. 4b). Alternatively,
we could say that “segregation” was transitional and short-lived because Ni diffused rapidly along
grain boundaries (fast diffusion pathways) and accumulated in the interstitial fcc grains of the core
(profile AA’ in Fig. 4a) and beyond the core outer border (profile CC’ in Fig. 4b).
Comment (8) The post-shock heating of above 600 °C locally in one bleb/feldspar does not conflict
with a lower overall post-shock temperature estimated from the bulk Hugoniot. Unless it was meant
to say the vesicular feldspars are pervasive and the bulk post-shock temperature is that high of >600
C, which would make a significant difference for the metamorphic petrography of the sample…
The high-temperature scenario is not only supported “locally in one bleb”, but also by additional
factors. These include the widespread (i.e., “pervasive” but not “ubiquitous”) distribution of vesicular
plagioclase glass (lines 145-147, lines S306-S317, Figs 3a and S6a,b) in meteorite NWA 479 but also
NWA 032 (Fig. S6c), the occurrence of Si-rich liquid blobs (lines 147-148, S318-S322, Figs 3b and
S6d), and the local but frequent melting of ilmenite and pyroxene (Fig. S6e,f). This indicates that
plagioclase (which constitutes 20-30 vol% of the rock) was still molten and hot (>1450°C) immedi-
ately after pressure release (lines 600-610). Then, an additional bleb has confirmed an equilibrium
peak-shock temperature >600°C (lines S622-S645 and point b of the response to comment 1).
Finally, the usual indicators of strong shock are numerous, including well-developed planar defor-
mation and mosaicism in olivine (lines S384-S385), unequivocal evidence for massive crystal-plastic
deformation in all the types of phenocrysts (see below and lines S385-S386), and large shock melt
veins. In conclusion, the observations indicate that the equilibrium peak-shock temperature in me-
teorite NWA 479 was high. Even the local preservation of high-pressure minerals does not invalidate
this statement (lines S333-S362 and the response to Reviewer #1).
Regarding the crystal-plastic deformation of silicates and oxides, we would like to bring to your
attention the fact that we have carried out EBSD maps on 11 olivine, 8 pyroxene, 7 ilmenite, and 6
chromite phenocrysts from our subsample of meteorite NWA 479 (not shown as dedicated to a spe-
cific paper). The majority of the phenocrysts show smooth, gradual, crystal-plastic deformation with
internal cumulative misorientations of up to several tens of degrees. These results provide further
compelling evidence that the rock experienced high peak-shock temperatures. Based on a compre-
hensive review of the available literature and my own experience, it is very unlikely that these min-
erals can undergo plastic deformation at low temperatures, particularly if the time is short. A specific
paper on the deformation of those phenocrysts will be submitted in the near future to confirm the
high peak-shock temperature proposed here. The decision to focus on the Fe-Ni metal blebs in the
present paper is a deliberate one, justified by the fact that the information is already very dense,
with a substantial amount of new data supported by a detailed supplementary file. Including EBSD
maps of silicates and oxides would densify the information even more, blur the message, and cer-
tainly not help to keep the reader on edge.
Finally, it is important to note that the reliability of whole-rock temperature estimates obtained
from the bulk Hugoniot is increasingly being questioned (Asimow et al., 2018; Hu and Sharp, 2022,
and references therein), especially for complex systems, in good agreement with the general com-
ments of Reviewer #1.
References cited in the responses to Reviewer #2
- Asimow, P.D. Melts under extreme conditions from shock experiments. In: Kono, Y. & Sanloup, C. (eds) Magmas Press. Elsevier,
Amsterdam, pp 387–418 (2018).
- Hu, J. & Sharp, T.G. Formation, preservation and extinction of high-pressure minerals in meteorites: temperature effects in
shock metamorphism and shock classification. Prog. Earth Planet. Sci. 9, 6 (2022).
- Kaufman, L. & Cohen, M. The martensitic transformation in the iron-nickel system. J. Met. 206, 1393-1401 (1956).
- Swartzendruber, L.J., Itkin, V.P. & Alcock, C.B. The Fe-Ni (iron-nickel) system. J. Phase Equilib. 12, 288-312 (1991).
- Yang, C.W., Williams, D.B. & Goldstein, J.I. A revision of the Fe-Ni phase diagram at low temperatures (≤400°C). J. Phase
Equilib. 17, 522-531 (1996).

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewer #3
The answers of the authors to the comments of the reviewers are exceptionally extensive, very
detailed, and well understandable. I will mainly comment on the replies of the authors to the two
reviewers.
Reviewer #1:
Comment 1a: Mesostasis vs impact melting: The textural arguments are convincing, especially be-
cause the authors confirm the presence of both vesicles and immiscible Si-rich liquids. They give also
characteristics of how to distinguish between both features on BSE images.
Comment 1b: Presence of high-pressure phases and the indicated peak pressure. The inhomogene-
ous presence of the latter from previous studies underlines El Goresy et al. (2013) red flag to use
them for peak pressure and the presence of very different P-T-t paths on a local scale.
Comment 1c: Thermal equilibrium: It seems, and the authors convincingly show the “sloppy” usage
of the term “equilibrium” in the planetary science community. Added text is sufficient to explain the
situation.
Comment 2: In my opinion, bcc, fcc. Martensitic transformation etc., should be also common terms
in the space science community and a reference to one of the many material science / metallography
textbook should have been sufficient. The explanation in the supplementary material is ok, except
that I would add that martensitic transformation have a low activation energy and need a small
driving force.
Spelling out the acronyms bcc, fcc, and hcp was a special request of Reviewer #1. We suggest
keeping the latest version unchanged (i.e., with the acronyms explained and the dedicated paragraph
in the supplementary materials), so that the unfamiliar readers have the information on hand. Then,
it is true that martensitic transformations generally have low activation energies and usually need a
small driving force to be initiated. However, as explained in lines 307-328, Mn-bearing but also Mn-
free Fe-Ni alloys are exceptions on that score, especially when fine-grained, C-poor and compressed
like here. In short, martensitic transformations in Fe-Ni materials need longer incubation times, and
higher activation energies and driving forces than other materials. Put differently: on an absolute
scale, the activation energy (in Joule) of martensitic transformations is low when compared to other
physicochemical reactions, but non-negligible when Fe-Ni alloys are considered.
A critical own comment: The authors use the term “lattice” but meaning “structure”. This error is
widespread and usually accepted. I would change nothing.
Reviewer #3 is right with this comment, but the use of “lattice” instead of “structure” is deliberate
here. The reason is that, in the EBSD community, the term “structure”, or sometimes “texture”, has
the meaning of “crystallographic preferred orientation (CPO)”, also referred to as… “lattice preferred
orientation (LPO)” in many texts. For example, saying that a given mineral phase has “a strong
texture/structure/CPO/LPO” means that the pole figures for that mineral show “strong clusters of
axes/poles”. From this perspective, there is no wording making consensus in all fields of Earth and
materials sciences. We also suggest not changing anything, as recommended by Reviewer #3.
Comment 3: Influence of alloying elements, use of average composition, statistical significance. The
treatment of alloying elements, grain size and compression are well done and understandable. The
authors have clarified that they have used average compositions not over the whole profile but for
plateaus along the profile.
Statistical significance: The statistical significance is somewhat reduced, but preparing more FIB
samples is not realistic. What may be criticized is that no error is given for the chemical analyses nor
for the constants in the equation 1-3 in the supplementary material, therefore no error propagation
calculation possible.
True, but uncertainties are discussed in lines S698-S707 and S710-S714. For example, we consider
ranges of values for solar absorptance, hemispherical emittance, orbital distance from the Sun, and
mass loss on atmospheric entry. In addition, we address the hypotheses of launch vs fall pairing to
calculate the meteorite mass. We also want to recall that equations 1-3 have been developed by
others with no clue on how to deal with error calculations in complex cases like here. In short, we
tackled the possible errors and uncertainties from a qualitative point of view, because doing it quan-
titatively would require a dedicated study.
Comment 4: Deformation process due to magmatic cooling vs. impact: The difference in the material
response of stress between metals vs. minerals and the actual observations in the sample are con-
vincing evidence that the authors are able to distinguish the results of magmatic cooling vs. impact.
Comment 5: ok

Line 205-207: References have been added.
